chapter_theme: The sarukkam's council scene continues. The minister Sachchutan first shows the Vidyadhara king the pleasure-city of Asvagriva, then names Asvagriva's parents, brothers and counsellors, his strength, the tribute he took and gave up, and urges that the girl be given to him; Bhavachutan then rises to speak and begins to name a fault.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara king's minister who speaks 277 to 306 in favour of giving the girl to Asvagriva
the second minister, who answers Sachchutan from 307
the Vidyadhara king, father of the girl, to whom both ministers speak
the discus-lord, son of Mayurakandan and Nilanganai, suitor for the girl
the Vidyadhara clans who fear Asvagriva
the kings who pay Asvagriva tribute
women who carry love-messages through the garland street
the astrologers who set down the girl's horoscope

287.reading: Young women, creeper-slender to men and praised for their small anklet-feet, have a custom of touching those feet to the flower-garlanded hair of their lovers, which tells of the lovers' quarrel.
287.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are hard to construe: தோய வைத்து ஊடல் உணர்த்தும் தொழில் may mean the woman sets her foot in the man's hair to show or to end her sulk. The reading follows the nearer sense and is held loosely.

288.reading: The broad chests of strong-armed men, smeared with red sandal, are pressed by the breasts of dark-eyed women, and the bees caught in the crushed paste cling and cry out.
288.nuance: முடவண் டிலைத்தடத் தேங்கும் இரக்கம் (line 3-4) is obscure; முடவண்டு could be a bee with a crushed wing, and the pity it draws is read here as a figure for the crushed paste.

289.reading: Women of full breasts, wearied, taste with their lovers the ripe fruits of love's joy, and many lift a curved brow in mock anger as desire mingles within them.
289.nuance: The ripe fruits (இன்பக் கனிகள்) are the pleasure itself, and the frowning brow is the sulk of lovers' play, not a real quarrel.

290.reading: Many men have drunk the nectar of coral lips and cannot match the women's appetite, so they tire, and the dark long-eyed women's languor is great.
290.nuance: The verse says men tire because they are not equal to the women (ஒவ்வாது இளைப்பர்), which turns the usual picture of the weary woman about.

291.reading: Waists seem to ache and droop, bees wander eating the fresh scent of buds in the women's wreathed hair, and a breeze moves through.

292.reading: A gem-dark bee, dyed by the red sandal of the women's breasts, sees its growing mate in the cloud-high grove and, unafraid, hides nearby.
292.nuance: The last two lines are compressed: அஞ்சா ஒளிக்கும் அயலது அதுவே is taken as the bee hiding unafraid beside its mate, a pairing that echoes the lovers.

293.reading: On beds of soft leaves in the grove, strings of gems slipped from the women's clothing, sandal paste and garlands lie in a heap over which swarms of bees press.
293.event: Lovers leave their gems, paste and garlands scattered over the leaf beds of the grove, and bees swarm over them.

294.reading: Go-between women with love-letters and wishing-tree garlands in jewelled caskets roam the garland street, and the speaker bids the king see how many there are.
294.nuance: கண்டாய் (line 4) is the speaker's own pointing-out: the sight is offered to the king as proof of the city's life.
294.event: Go-between women carry love-letters and garlands through the garland street.

295.reading: Garlands snap and golden vessels ring out as anklet-wearing men churn the sea of desire among the women; their doings are marked as wicked.
295.nuance: தீமைத் தொழிலவை தேர்ந்துள வன்றே (line 4) can be read as an aside that these doings are faulty, or as the poet's tag for such deeds being ready to hand; the sense is not fixed, and no claim is built on it.

296.reading: The speaker names Asvagriva's line: his father Mayurakandan, a king as majestic as Indra over the golden city, and his mother Nilanganai, a chief queen who shines among the wives.
296.nuance: This opens the minister's turn from the city to its lord; the earlier verses of the sarukkam give no speaker name, and the speaker is Sachchutan only from 307.

297.reading: Asvagriva, lord of the garlanded spear, took up the discus, bowed the mountains that moon-skim, and the earth fell in with his will.
297.event: Asvagriva wins the discus and brings the hill-kings, and then the land, under his will.

298.reading: No king is his equal in strength of kin, in the discus he rules by, in the parasol of victory, in lineage, in learned vidya and in finishing what he plans.

claims.claim: a king's standing rests on kin, lineage, learning, the discus and the finishing of what he plans

299.reading: The speaker names Asvagriva's three younger brothers: Nilakandan, Vairamakandan and Sukandan.
299.nuance: The edition gives this verse three lines; a fourth is lost or was never cut.

300.reading: In the army, its calm order and the share of food, and in other manifold things, none equals him; the discus he rules by is held without a country to answer to, and the speaker says that if he is pleased the world would pass to others.
300.nuance: The army and the food are two of the limbs the Kural counts (381). நடையவன் உவப்பின் ஞாலம் பிறருழை நடப்ப தென்றான் (line 4) is hard to place and may mean that the world will go over to others' side if he is pleased.

301.reading: Arimanju is his minister of the law-treatise, able to bring learned men round to his word; Satavindu, great-natured, is skilled in the omen-books; no learned man sees his equal.
301.nuance: The minister's mastery is told wholly in books (ஆணைநூல், நூல், நிமித்தம்), with no word for native wit.

302.reading: A man of pity says that those who lean on him honour no god but him and have no kin but him; the earth rains wealth for him, and all kings bow to none other.
302.nuance: The subject of lines 1 and 2 is unclear: it could be Satavindu of 301 or Asvagriva himself, and தன்னலால் தெய்வம் பேணார் (line 1) may mean they honour no god other than him.

303.reading: In his youth the sword-bearer lifted and rolled like a toy a heap of rock that two hundred elephants might have raised, so that the faultless-learned Vidyadharas took fright.
303.nuance: The subject is named only by the title of the sword-bearer, குமாரகாலம், his youth; the verse is read as about Asvagriva.
303.event: The young Asvagriva lifts and rolls a mass of rock that two hundred elephants could raise, and the Vidyadharas fear him.

304.reading: Because of his full austerity no king of the sea-girt earth fails to heed his command; fearing his anger they paid tribute and sent word, and all that was ours was lost before the girl of good austerity appeared.
304.nuance: நாம் மாண்டது எல்லாம் (line 4) may mean everything we lost, or all that passed before her birth; the sense is not fixed. The claim in line 1 is a courtier's, put to win the king, and the work does not here answer it.
304.event: The kings, fearing Asvagriva's anger, pay tribute and send word to him.

claims.claim: complete austerity in a past life brings a ruler the obedience of all kings

305.reading: Since the girl, the creeper of the speaker's own family, was born, Asvagriva has grown kind and stopped taking tribute, and the speaker asks the king to say whether he has told anything untrue.
305.nuance: The speaker's own reckoning is that the girl's birth is why Asvagriva softened; the verse does not say whether the girl's beauty or her line is the cause.
305.event: After the girl's birth Asvagriva gives up taking tribute from the Vidyadharas.

306.reading: The speaker says the girl is fit for Asvagriva, that his mind is set and firm, that the Vidyadharas fear him, and asks whether, if the king is willing, giving her would not be good.
306.nuance: Bhavachutan answers in 308 to 310, but the argument is not finished in this chapter, so the claim is left as reported, not refuted.
306.event: The minister urges the Vidyadhara king to give his daughter to Asvagriva.

claims.claim: it is wise and good to give the girl to the suitor whom all fear

307.reading: When Sachchutan, whom the king of the golden-mounted elephant honours, has spoken, Bhavachutan rises to speak.
307.nuance: This verse names the two ministers, and so fixes that the speaker of 277 to 306 was Sachchutan.
307.event: Bhavachutan takes up the debate after Sachchutan has spoken.

308.reading: Bhavachutan says that Sachchutan, learned and quick to judge, wise in sifting and strong of tongue, says nothing that is not true, and that nothing he has said is excess.
308.nuance: He first grants his colleague's learning and truthfulness, and turns in 309.

309.reading: Bhavachutan says he too saw Asvagriva's worth, but he saw one fault in this proud warrior, and he will not join in without speaking it out.
309.nuance: The fault itself is named only after this chapter. ஒட்டினும் ஒட்டேன் (line 4) is read as refusing to join the colleague's view while holding back this point.
309.event: Bhavachutan declares that he has found a fault in Asvagriva and will state it.

claims.claim: a counsellor must voice a fault he has seen, even against a colleague's agreed praise

310.reading: When the lady of the wreath was born, those who know the excellence of the sky's planets, faultless in their craft, laid the birth-horoscope leaf in the place of the giving-planet.
310.nuance: தானக் கோளிற் சாதக வோலை தலைவைத்தார் (line 4) is read as placing the leaf under the planet of giving; the horoscope's content is not told here.
310.event: On the day the girl is born, astrologers draw up her birth horoscope.

links.note: Verse 304 says the kings paid tribute in fear of his anger; verse 305 says that since the girl was born he has stopped taking it.
links.teaches: The same overlord appears first as one who is paid in fear and then as one who waives his due, so the girl's birth is given as a political turning and the courting rests on that change.

links.note: Verse 305 reckons the girl's birth as the moment Asvagriva softened; verse 310 gives the birth as the moment the astrologers set down her horoscope.
links.teaches: One birth is read twice, by a minister as the cause of a change in the suitor and by an astrologer as the moment her fate was fixed, so the story weighs politics against the stars.

links.note: Verse 308 vouches for Sachchutan's truth and learning; verse 309 says the speaker saw a fault and will not stay silent.
links.teaches: The second minister grants his colleague's praise and then withholds assent in the same breath, so agreement on facts does not carry agreement on the verdict.

links.note: Bhavachutan says that he saw a fault and will speak though the other has praised; Kural 638 says the one at the king's side must speak what is good even if the king is ignorant.
links.teaches: The couplet binds a minister to speak against a king's folly, and the scene shows the harder case where he speaks against a fellow minister's persuasive counsel.

gains.a: The minister's refusal to join the praise gets a stated rule, so his dissent reads as a duty and not as rivalry.
gains.b: The rule meets a case in which the one to be corrected is a colleague already trusted by the king, not the king himself.

links.note: The minister lists Asvagriva's army, its order and the food supply among the reasons none equals him; Kural 381 counts army, people, resources, ministers, friends and fort as a king's six limbs.
links.teaches: The minister's praise follows the Kural's list for army and food but adds the discus, the lineage and learning, so the poet counts as kingly worth what the Kural's checklist leaves out.

gains.a: The speaker's list of army, food and ministers gets a stated standard of what a complete king must have.
gains.b: The couplet's six limbs meet a king whose praise adds lineage, learning and a magic discus, so its checklist is tested against what a court poet values.

links.note: The minister's praise rests on law-treatise, omen-books and learning; Kural 636 says that natural wit joined to treatises cannot be matched by any scheme.
links.teaches: The poem's model minister is made by treatises alone, where the couplet gives native wit the first place, so the court poet and the Kural weigh a counsellor differently.

gains.a: The minister's praise gets a measure that asks what books alone can do without native wit.
gains.b: The couplet's pairing of wit and learning meets a counsellor described only by learning, so it is tested against a case where one half is missing.

links.note: The Vidyadhara kings pay tribute and send word out of fear of Asvagriva's anger; Kural 680 says those of small domains, afraid, bow to the great and take what is offered.
links.teaches: The kings' tribute is the couplet's counsel carried out, but the minister then asks for the girl to be given, which shows how bowing to a great king can end in a marriage and not only in a payment.

gains.a: The tribute out of fear gets a name in policy: the small bowing to the great for what they can get.
gains.b: The couplet's bowing is shown running on from tribute into the giving of a daughter, a cost it does not name.

links.note: Verse 289 names the pleasures of lovers as ripe fruits they taste; Tirumanthiram 201 names a man's wife as the ripe jackfruit he will not eat while he toils for the wild date.
links.teaches: Both speak of sexual joy as fruit, but the poem lets lovers eat it freely in the grove while the Tirumanthiram asks whose fruit it is, so the image carries opposite moral weights.

gains.a: The fruit image gets a question the verse leaves unasked, whose fruit it is and whether it is one's own to eat.
gains.b: The jackfruit image meets a scene of lovers who eat the ripe fruit freely, so the verse is seen against the pleasure it warns about.

source_issues: 299 has three lines (the edition's own count); one line is probably lost.
300 line 4 நடையவன் is hard to construe; reading is held loosely.
The speaker of 287 to 306 is named only at 307 (சச்சுதன்); the addressee is fixed from 277 in the previous chapter, where the speaker offers to tell the king of the girl's suitor.
